verdict: OK to lend in Kottayam tyres and rubber products, but only to converters and niche makers who can pass through record rubber prices; avoid commodity tyre makers and anyone with unhedged raw-material exposure.
title: Kottayam tyres & rubber products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Kottayam is a rubber town before it is a tyre town: the trade here is RSS-4 sheet, and the local price has just set a record at ₹284.50 per kg, above the previous ₹284 of August 1 [3], with a local report putting it at ₹300 per kg [1].** A converter buys sheet or latex, compounds it, and sells solid tyres, industrial pneumatics, press-on bands, mats and moulded goods; cash comes in from replacement and tier-I/OEM buyers, not from the sheet trade itself. The value sits in compounding skill and the customer relationship, not in the raw material, which is priced daily and publicly. ## What has changed now
**The input has become the story: record sheet prices driven by tyre-maker demand against a supply shortage [2][3] squeeze exactly the borrowers who cannot reprice.** Peer tyre makers are expanding capacity on near-full utilisation while margins fall, and are answering with staggered price increases and richer product mix [4][6]. So when a proposal lands, check the last four quarters of gross margin against the RSS-4 price line; if margin held while sheet rose, ask for the price-revision letters to customers. ## Where the growth is
**Pursue converters selling into material handling, industrial and export niches, the segment where a rated peer grew TOI 19% in FY25 on volume and realisation [11].** The national demand base is real: replacement is about 70% of volumes and exports about 25% [10], and IIP for NIC 22 is up 21.4% YoY with exports up 17.1% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. Kerala's GST collections are running 4.2 pp faster than India [D]. Avoid pure commodity tyre makers and anyone whose entire output is one standard SKU sold on price; they cannot pass ₹284.50 [3] through. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against the raw-material cycle, not the P&L: keep the working-capital limit tied to a stock-and-debtor statement, and take the sheet purchase register every month.** Take monthly: RSS-4 landed cost versus sale-price revisions, stock days, and top-five buyer concentration. Covenant a minimum gross margin and a maximum raw-material inventory days; if either breaches, freeze the non-fund-based limit first. Collect from customer the split of domestic versus export sales and the share of business on annual price contracts. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch for margin compression arriving one quarter after a sheet spike, and for debtors stretching as buyers push back on price rises.** If receivable days cross the pre-spike average, ask for the ageing and the buyer-wise revision status. If a borrower starts buying sheet forward without matching sales contracts, treat it as speculation, not hedging. Local coverage of this city's own manufacturing base is thin; the sources are price reports, so lean on first principles and the peer set above.
watch: Monthly: RSS-4 landed cost vs sale-price revision log
Sheet up two months with no revision -> cut limit utilisation by a step
Below covenant -> freeze non-fund-based limit, reprice
Rising while sales flat -> ask for forward purchase contracts
Monthly: debtor days and top-five buyer share
Debtor days above pre-spike average -> obtain ageing and buyer-wise status
Quarterly: capacity utilisation and order book
Utilisation falling with stock building -> shift to stock statement review
